title: Message Queues and Event Streams
summary: Choose between work queues and replayable logs, then define partition keys, delivery semantics, dead-letter handling and lag limits.
body:
Most designs eventually need to hand work from one component to another without making the caller wait: send the welcome email, transcode the upload, update the feed, recompute the leaderboard. A message broker decouples the producer from the consumer in time, in rate and in failure. In an interview the useful question is not "should I add Kafka?" but "what is the contract between these two components?": does each message represent a task that one worker should complete, or an event that many independent readers should see in order and possibly replay? That distinction picks the technology, and it determines how you talk about ordering, duplicates and lag.

## Queue versus log

A **work queue** (Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ classic queues) hands each message to one consumer. When the consumer acknowledges it, the broker deletes it. Unacknowledged messages become visible again after a timeout (SQS calls this the visibility timeout, default 30 seconds) or when the consumer's connection drops (RabbitMQ). Workers compete for messages, so you scale by adding workers, and there is no notion of going back in time.

A **log** or **stream** (Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Redpanda, Pulsar topics) appends records to an ordered, durable sequence and does not delete them when they are read. Each reader keeps its own position, called an offset. Many independent applications can read the same records at their own pace, and a reader can rewind to reprocess history.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph WQ["Work queue"]
        P1["Producer"] --> Q[["Queue"]]
        Q -->|"msg 1"| W1["Worker A"]
        Q -->|"msg 2"| W2["Worker B"]
    end
    subgraph LOG["Log / stream"]
        P2["Producer"] --> L[["Topic partition: 0 1 2 3 4 5"]]
        L -->|"offset 5"| C1["Search indexer"]
        L -->|"offset 2"| C2["Analytics job"]
    end
```

On the left, messages 1 and 2 go to different workers and disappear once acknowledged. On the right, the same records stay in the log; the search indexer has read up to offset 5 while the analytics job is behind at offset 2, and neither affects the other. Use a queue for tasks ("resize this image") and a log for facts ("order 42 was placed") that several systems react to.

## Partitions, ordering and consumer groups

A single ordered log cannot scale indefinitely, so Kafka splits a topic into **partitions**. A producer picks the partition by hashing the record key, so all records with the same key (for example `order_id`) land in the same partition in the order they were written. Kafka guarantees order within a partition, never across partitions. If you need every event for one user processed in order, key by user ID; if you key randomly you get even load and no ordering.

A **consumer group** is a set of consumers sharing the work for one application. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at a time, so a group's useful parallelism is capped by the partition count: 12 partitions and 20 consumers leaves 8 idle. Different groups each receive every record.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PR["Producers: key = order_id"] --> P0[["Partition 0"]]
    PR --> P1[["Partition 1"]]
    PR --> P2[["Partition 2"]]
    subgraph G1["Group: billing"]
        B1["Consumer 1"]
        B2["Consumer 2"]
    end
    subgraph G2["Group: email"]
        E1["Consumer 1"]
    end
    P0 --> B1
    P1 --> B1
    P2 --> B2
    P0 --> E1
    P1 --> E1
    P2 --> E1
```

The billing group splits three partitions across two consumers; the email group has one consumer reading all three. If billing consumer 2 dies, the group rebalances and consumer 1 takes partition 2, resuming from the last committed offset. Choose partition count from target throughput and consumer parallelism with headroom, because increasing it later changes which partition a key hashes to and breaks per-key ordering for in-flight keys.

Queues have equivalents: SQS FIFO queues order messages within a **message group ID** and process different groups in parallel, while SQS standard queues offer only best-effort ordering. Hot keys are the classic failure: one celebrity's events all hash to one partition and one consumer, so that partition lags while the others idle.

## Offsets, acknowledgements and delivery semantics

Delivery semantics come from *when* the consumer records progress relative to doing the work.

- **At-most-once**: commit the offset (or acknowledge) before processing. A crash after the commit loses the message.
- **At-least-once**: process, then commit. A crash between the two causes redelivery, so the consumer sees duplicates. This is the normal default.
- **Effectively-once**: at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent or transactional effect. Kafka transactions can atomically write output records and consumer offsets *within Kafka*, and SQS FIFO deduplicates sends within a 5-minute window, but neither extends to an external API or a separate database. You still need idempotent consumers, as covered in the idempotency lesson.

Because a log keeps records, **replay** is a feature: deploy a fixed consumer, reset the group's offsets to yesterday, and rebuild a derived view. That only works if retention covers the window. Kafka retains by time or size per topic (the broker default is 7 days), and **log compaction** keeps only the latest record per key, which is useful for changelog topics. SQS retains messages for 4 days by default, up to 14.

## Poison messages and dead-letter queues

A message that always fails (bad schema, a bug, a deleted referenced row) will be retried forever and block progress. In a queue it burns worker time; in a log partition it blocks every record behind it, because the consumer cannot commit past it. Bound retries and then move the message to a **dead-letter queue** (DLQ): SQS does this with a redrive policy after `maxReceiveCount` receives, RabbitMQ with a dead-letter exchange, and Kafka applications usually publish to a separate retry or DLQ topic themselves. A DLQ needs an owner, an alert on its depth and a tool to redrive messages after the fix; otherwise it is just a slower way to lose data.

## Backpressure and lag

A broker absorbs bursts but cannot fix a sustained deficit. If producers publish 50,000 events per second and consumers process 40,000, backlog grows by 10,000 per second, or 36 million per hour. The key metric is **consumer lag**: the difference between the newest offset and the group's committed offset, or the age of the oldest message in a queue. Age matters more than count because it maps directly to user-visible staleness.

Responses, in order of preference: scale consumers (up to the partition count), make each message cheaper (batch database writes), shed or sample low-value work, and finally push back on producers by rejecting at the edge. Limit consumer prefetch (RabbitMQ `basic.qos`, Kafka `max.poll.records`) so one slow consumer does not hoard messages, and keep processing time under the visibility timeout or poll interval, or the broker will assume the consumer died and redeliver.

## Choosing a broker

| Need | Good fit | Why | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Background tasks, one worker each | SQS standard, RabbitMQ | Per-message ack, simple scaling, built-in DLQ | No replay; standard SQS can reorder and duplicate |
| Per-entity ordering for tasks | SQS FIFO, RabbitMQ single active consumer | Ordered per group | Lower throughput per group; one slow group stalls itself |
| Events consumed by many services | Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar | Fan-out by consumer group, replay, high throughput | Partition planning, rebalances, operational cost |
| Change data capture into search/cache | Kafka with compaction | Ordered per key, rebuildable views | Schema evolution, retention vs rebuild time |
| Request needs an answer now | No queue; synchronous call | Caller is waiting anyway | Queue adds latency and a polling or callback path |

## When not to add a queue

A queue is not free. It adds a hop, an eventually consistent boundary, a new failure mode (the broker) and a harder debugging story. Skip it when the caller needs the result to continue, when the work takes milliseconds and the downstream has ample capacity, or when the only reason is "it scales". Also avoid dual writes: writing to the database and then publishing to Kafka from application code can commit one and lose the other. Use a transactional outbox or CDC from the database log instead.

## Common interview mistakes

- Saying "Kafka guarantees ordering" without naming the partition key.
- Claiming exactly-once delivery end to end.
- Adding consumers beyond the partition count and expecting more throughput.
- Ignoring the poison-message path and DLQ ownership.
- Forgetting that an asynchronous boundary changes the API: the client now needs a job ID, status endpoint or push notification.

## How to use it in an interview

Name the boundary first: "Upload acknowledges once the file is in object storage; transcoding is a task on a queue, so the API returns 202 with a job ID." Then state the contract in one sentence each: the key that determines ordering, the delivery semantics and how the consumer makes duplicates harmless, retention and replay needs, and the lag you will alert on. Numbers that matter: events per second, average message size (Kafka handles megabytes per second per partition comfortably; very large payloads belong in object storage with a pointer in the message), and the acceptable end-to-end delay. Expect follow-ups such as "a consumer is down for an hour, what happens?", "how do you reprocess after a bug?", and "what if one key is 100 times hotter than the rest?".

## Interview exercise

A ride-sharing app publishes trip events (requested, accepted, started, completed) that billing, notifications and analytics all consume. Choose the broker type, the partition key and a partition count for 20,000 events per second if one consumer handles 2,000 per second. Explain what happens to billing if a completed event arrives twice, and how you would rebuild the analytics tables after discovering a bug from three days ago.

## Further reading

- [Apache Kafka documentation: design](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#design) covers partitions, consumer groups, delivery semantics and log compaction.
- [Amazon SQS Developer Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html) documents visibility timeouts, FIFO message groups and dead-letter queues.
- [RabbitMQ: consumer acknowledgements and publisher confirms](https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms) explains acknowledgement and prefetch behavior.
keyTakeaways: Use a work queue for tasks one worker should complete and a log for events many consumers read and may replay.
Ordering exists only within a partition or message group, so the partition key is a design decision.
A consumer group's parallelism is capped by the partition count.
At-least-once delivery is the realistic default; make the consumer's effect idempotent.
Bound retries with a dead-letter queue and alert on consumer lag measured as age, not just count.
